Hi! I opened a PR adding Mathlib/Probability/HypothesisTesting/NeymanPearson.lean, formalizing the classical Neyman-Pearson lemma with reference Ingster, Y. and Suslina, I.A., 2012. Nonparametric goodness-of-fit testing under Gaussian models (Vol. 169).

We state the theorem in the weighted form ∫ T dP + t * ∫ (1 - T) dQ, over measurable tests T : Ω → ℝ with values in [0, 1], using P + Q as the canonical dominating measure; rather than starting with the constrained formulation that fixes the Type I error and minimizes the Type II error. The reasons are two fold.

First, it can be thought as the Lagrangian form of the classical constrained Neyman-Pearson problem.

Second, this weighted form is often arises in applications, such as, in minimax lower-bound arguments for functional estimation, where one typically reduces estimation lower bounds to testing inequalities involving weighted sums of error probabilities.

This work is co-authored-by: Rajarshi Mukherjee @Rajarshi Mukherjee

Feedback on the location, formulation, or naming would be very welcome!!
Hi! Can you comment on whether you used AI for your work (and if so, edit the PR description to describe how --- as detailed in mathlib's AI guidelines)? Thanks!
Thanks for the reminder! I already included a statement on AI use, please let me know if you have any specific quetsion! thanls!
Can you be a bit more specific? Did you write all code by hand, and then used Claude for advice on naming? Did Claude generate any of the code, etc. Thanks.

It looks like generated to me (or you unfortunately followed bad AI code style). The usual advice I give in this case is

  • Collaps the wall of haves
  • Format the code as 100 letters per line
  • break the proof into smaller lemmas

we first manually wrote a blueprint in latex with every definition and lemma we need
NL_Blueprint_NP_Lemma.pdf then we checked the Mathlib API with claude code, chatgpt and LeanSearch, We manually wrote the outline with sorries and finished the proof with haves, since we are unfamiliar with mathlib naming style, we used claude code skill for proof golfing and some syntax preference, eg whether should use unfold or simp only [];

If you believe the math to be trivial, it is more of a reason for there to be less lines!

If you believe your sub-lemmas are too trivial and will never be used ( note that we have lemmas that state x+0 = 0, they may not be used directly that often but very often by tactics) you may label them as “private” .

Ideally a proof should be no longer than ten lines , is the rough estimate I’ve read.

Typically you will want some helper lemmas that are then used by tactics to dispense of “trivial math” .

It may be somewhat more opaque but if the math is not insightful this can still be readable , and sometimes more so ( you can read <tactic> [arguments..] as “it follows from basic manipulation of said arguments via tactic “, use naming conventions to then read the arguments.)

Thank you so much for the message! Learnt a lot about the style, actually I do have a version breaking things into private lemmas (eg, measurability stuff...), but i am confused at the criteria/rule for breaking and just abandoned that version (any golden standard or rubrics for this?). I ll try to break again and come back to this PR!

Ideally a proof should be no longer than ten lines , is the rough estimate I’ve read.

There are legitimate reasons to have proofs that are 20, 30 lines. But these are one in a hundred, or even rarer. They're the big results that usually get names or build entire theories.
Anything past 30 or so lines should either be golfed or be split into lemmas.

Violeta Hernández said:

Anything past 30 or so lines should either be golfed or be split into lemmas.

There are also exceptions for this, but these are also rare. If your proof is longer than that, chances are high it can either be golfed to make it shorter, split into smaller lemmas --- or (in the rare case) the proof should be commented to outline what's going on.

My first thought when reading your PR was that this weighted sum of integrals can be written using avgRisk for a binary parameter space and the zero-one loss and that you are showing that a particular estimator attains the bayesRisk, and then I remembered that I proved a form of your result in a PR I opened a year ago, #27579 (big overview PR from which I split smaller parts in new PRs).
I stopped making the effort of merging that material to Mathlib because I got distracted by other projects, and also because for some other results in the PR it would be better to have measurable selection theorems in Mathlib, which we don't have yet (I've since proved some of those in the Brownian Motion project which I need to upstream).

I took some time to update #27579 today (and split a new PR #39810 for the Bayes estimator definitions).
My version of your result is isBayesEstimator_binaryBayesEstimator, in the Binary file of that PR. Your test has a parameter \eta, but I just took the particular case of \eta = 0 (or 1? I'm not sure, I took something arbitrary for the equality case).
